name: Capixyl

lead: Capixyl is a cosmetic ingredient combining a peptide with red clover extract, sold for use in anti-hair-loss serums.
The supplier cites reduced shedding, but the available sources give few independent human data.

paras: Claimed to improve follicle anchoring via collagen and laminin, and to inhibit 5-alpha reductase through biochanin A; lab-level support cited by Grokipedia is at high concentrations.
No specific adverse effects are documented in the sources; it is regulated as a cosmetic and is not an approved treatment for hair loss.

studies.title: Topical Alternatives for Hair Loss: Beyond the Conventional.

lead: Capixyl is a trademarked cosmetic active ingredient from Lucas Meyer Cosmetics, now part of Clariant, used in hair-loss serums. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as a combination of the peptide acetyl tetrapeptide-3 with red clover (Trifolium pratense) flower extract standardized for the isoflavone biochanin A. [1]

The supplier claims it reduces shedding by anchoring follicles, moderating DHT and limiting inflammation. [1] The sources found offer few independent human data: much of the quoted efficacy comes from supplier material or from tests of a three-ingredient combination rather than Capixyl alone. [1][2]
infobox: Cosmetic active ingredient (peptide plus plant extract)
Acetyl tetrapeptide-3, red clover extract (biochanin A) [1]

paras: Per Grokipedia, acetyl tetrapeptide-3 is said to raise collagen III and laminin in fibroblasts to improve follicle anchorage, while biochanin A is credited with inhibiting 5-alpha reductase. The source cites an in vitro assay at a high concentration for that last claim and notes it is not evidence of an effect on scalp DHT in users. [1]
Some web sources confuse Capixyl with Procapil, which contains biotinoyl tripeptide-1; they are separate products from different suppliers. [1]

No independent published trial of Capixyl on its own was found. A 2025 review of topical hair-growth products lists Capixyl among heavily marketed actives and discusses the clinical evidence available for such ingredients. [2] Grokipedia mentions an open-label comparison with 5% minoxidil of a combination of Redensyl, Capixyl and Procapil, in which more combination users were reported as improved; it notes that sample size and blinding details are absent and that the test did not isolate Capixyl. [1]

Grokipedia says supplier assessments report no local adverse reactions, without naming a specific study. It describes Capixyl as a cosmetic ingredient, so products cannot be approved as hair-loss drugs. [1]
